passages.t: ‘The LORD is my light and my salvation’, and ‘one thing I have asked’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David” (verse 1). Then two questions that answer themselves. “The LORD is my light and my salvation”, he says, and asks, “whom shall I fear?” Again: “The LORD is the stronghold of my life”, so “whom shall I dread?” (verse 1).

He has seen enemies fall before. “When the wicked came upon me to devour my flesh, my enemies and foes stumbled and fell” (verse 2). So even now, “Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear” (verse 3).

Then he names the one thing he wants most. “One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple” (verse 4).

God's house is his hiding place. “For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter; He will conceal me under the cover of His tent; He will set me high upon a rock” (verse 5). And he will answer with songs (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Light in the ancient world meant life, safety and favour. Darkness meant danger and death. Many psalms link God with light, but this one makes it personal: ‘my light’.

A stronghold was a fortified place to run to. A rock was a high place enemies could not climb.

Verse 5 pictures the sanctuary as a refuge. In Israel a person in danger could run to God's altar and take hold of its horns, the raised corners, and ask for protection. When Adonijah feared King Solomon, he “went to take hold of the horns of the altar” (1 Kings 1:50). The psalmist wants more than a moment of safety. He wants to live with God.

‘To gaze on the beauty of the LORD’ is one of the warmest lines in the Psalms. He does not only want God's help. He wants God.
passages.later:
John's Gospel opens with the same light: “The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it” (John 1:5). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And John writes, “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5).

Jesus praised Mary of Bethany for choosing one thing, as verse 4 does: “only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion” (Luke 10:42).

Hebrews uses words like verse 1: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (Hebrews 13:6).
passages.hard:
‘My heart will not fear’ (verse 3). Is fear a sign of weak faith?

The psalm does not say that. Read on, and the same man prays in anguish in verses 7 to 12. Courage in the Bible is not the absence of fear. It is trust that holds when fear is present. Verse 1 asks ‘whom shall I fear?’ because there is something to fear. The answer is not ‘nothing’. It is ‘the LORD is my light’.
passages.asks:
Verse 4 asks you a clear question. If you could ask God for one thing, what would it be? The psalmist asks for God himself.

Try sitting with the phrase ‘to gaze on the beauty of the LORD’. Prayer is not only asking for things. It can be simply looking.

passages.t: ‘Seek His face’, and ‘Wait patiently for the LORD’
passages.happening:
The tone changes. Now it is a plea. “Hear, O LORD, my voice when I call; be merciful and answer me” (verse 7).

He remembers an inner call: “My heart said, ‘Seek His face.’ Your face, O LORD, I will seek” (verse 8). And he fears losing that face: “Hide not Your face from me, nor turn away Your servant in anger” (verse 9).

Then one of the tenderest lines in the Psalms: “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (verse 10).

He is in danger in a court of lies: “false witnesses rise up against me, breathing out violence” (verse 12). Yet he says, “Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living” (verse 13). And he ends by speaking to himself, or to us: “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The two halves of Psalm 27 sound so different, confidence and then lament, that many scholars think two psalms were joined. Others think it was written as one, since the same words run through both halves, such as ‘salvation’ (verses 1 and 9) and ‘heart’ (verses 3, 8 and 14). Either way, the order teaches something. Confidence does not mean the trouble is over.

Verse 10 speaks into one of the deepest fears of that world. A person's family was their safety, their name and their protection in court. To be left by father and mother was to be left with nothing. The verse may describe something that happened, or imagine the worst that could happen. Either way it promises that God takes in the one whom even family has left, as a near relative takes in his own.

‘The land of the living’ means this life, here and now. He expects to see God's goodness before he dies, not only after.
passages.later:
God speaks the same promise through Isaiah. He asks whether a mother could forget her nursing child, and answers, “Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” (Isaiah 49:15).

At his trial Jesus faced the same kind of attack as verse 12: “many false witnesses came forward” (Matthew 26:60). And the call of verse 14 echoes God's word to Joshua: be strong and courageous, “Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9).
passages.hard:
‘Though my father and mother forsake me’ (verse 10). This verse can be very hard to read for anyone whose parents did leave them, or hurt them, or were never there.

The psalm does not pretend that does not happen. It names it. And it does not say the hurt is small. It says that the LORD ‘will receive’ you, the word for gathering someone in and taking them home. Being received by God does not erase what a parent did. It means you are not, in the end, unwanted.

If old wounds from your family still weigh on you, it can help a great deal to talk with someone you trust: a pastor, a counsellor or a wise friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
Psalm 27 asks you to seek God's face, not only his hand. Verse 8 is a good morning prayer: ‘Your face, O LORD, I will seek.’

And it asks you to wait. Notice that the psalm ends before the answer comes. ‘Wait patiently for the LORD’ is said twice, because once is rarely enough.
